children.text: CMS released preliminary AHEAD Model Year One performance data in January 2026, covering Maryland’s established Total Cost of Care program and the four initial AHEAD states: Vermont, Colorado, Connecticut, and New York. The data creates a clear bifurcation between hospitals that invested in care coordination infrastructure before entering the model and those that did not.
The Bifurcation: Who Is Winning and Who Is Absorbing Risk

Among rural hospitals in AHEAD states, 34% generated net shared savings in Year One, with an average positive variance of $1.4M against their total cost of care benchmark. These hospitals shared three characteristics: they had implemented a care transitions program at least 24 months before AHEAD entry, they had risk-stratified their Medicaid populations using SDOH data, and they had renegotiated at least one commercial payer contract to align incentives with the AHEAD benchmark.

The 41% of rural AHEAD participants that reported downside risk exposure in Year One averaged a negative variance of $880,000. The primary driver was higher-than-benchmarked specialist utilization—patients who previously had no primary care relationship presenting with advanced chronic disease and requiring expensive specialty workups. This is a predictable first-year effect that dissipates in Year Two as care coordination begins to intercept high-cost events.
The hospitals generating savings in AHEAD Year One had been building care coordination capacity for two to three years before entry. The model rewards preparation, not just participation.

body.title: AHEAD Year One Financial Performance: Rural Hospital Cohort

children.text: For rural hospitals currently evaluating AHEAD entry in the 2027 enrollment window, the data suggests a minimum 18–24 month preparation period before assuming performance risk. The investment threshold for a viable care coordination program—typically one full-time care coordinator per 500 high-risk attributed patients—runs between $280,000 and $420,000 annually for an average rural hospital population. Against potential shared savings of $1.4M, this is a strong return, but it requires upfront capital that many distressed rural hospitals do not have.

CFO ALERT: RHT program states offer care coordination infrastructure grants that can offset 40–60% of the upfront investment required before AHEAD entry. Check your state’s RHT funding allocation before assuming self-funding is the only path.

children.text: Five Actions for Rural Hospitals Targeting 2027 AHEAD Entry
Conduct total cost of care baseline analysis against CMS benchmark methodology immediately
Risk-stratify attributed Medicaid population using SDOH data before enrollment
Hire care coordinator(s) no later than Q1 2026 to build 18-month pre-entry track record
Renegotiate one commercial payer contract to include quality bonuses aligned with AHEAD metrics
Apply for RHT care coordination infrastructure funding by June 2026 enrollment deadline

summary: The CMS AHEAD (All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development) Model completed its first full measurement year in December 2025. Preliminary financial data from Maryland’s mature iteration and the four AHEAD pilot states reveals a bifurcation: hospitals with strong care coordination infrastructure are generating shared savings, while those without are absorbing downside risk they were not financially prepared to bear.
title: AHEAD Model Year One: Early Financial Outcomes and the Lessons Rural Hospital CFOs Cannot Afford to Miss
